segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For every high priest, taken from among people, is appointed on behalf of people in matters relating to God, to offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, since he himself is also beset by weakness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and because of it he is obliged to offer sacrifice for sins, as for the people, so also for himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron also was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest; it was the one who said to him,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “You are my Son; today I have become your father,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as he also says in another place,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “You are a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the days of his flesh he offered prayers and pleas, with a loud cry and tears, to the one who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Son though he was, he learned obedience from what he suffered,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and, having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: designated by God high priest in the order of Melchizedek.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become sluggish in hearing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the first elements of God’s oracles; you have come to need milk, not solid food.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For everyone who lives on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, since that person is an infant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But solid food is for the mature, those who because of their mature state have their faculties trained to distinguish good from evil.

notes.note: The verb means to keep one's feelings within measure, and in period usage especially to hold anger in check. It is a cooler word than the 'sympathize' used of Jesus in 4:15: the ordinary high priest restrains his severity toward sinners because he shares their weakness. 'Ignorant and going astray' echoes the Law's category of unintentional sins, for which sacrifice was provided.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest first offered a bull for his own sins and those of his household before offering for the people (Leviticus 16). The author will later contrast this with Jesus, who had no sin of his own to offer for.

notes.phrase: today I have become your father
notes.note: The quotation is Psalm 2:7, where God addresses Israel's king at his enthronement. 'Begotten' is the long-standing English rendering, but the word is now archaic. Several modern versions give the same sense with 'become your father'. The Greek verb is the ordinary one for a father producing a child.

The quotation is Psalm 110:4. The Greek word can mean a rank or class, or more loosely a kind or manner. Many scholars think the sense here is 'of the same kind as Melchizedek', since the author later paraphrases it as 'in the likeness of Melchizedek' (7:15). 'Order' should not suggest a succession of priests, because Melchizedek has no predecessors or successors in Scripture.

notes.traditional: in that he feared; because of his reverent submission
notes.note: The Greek word can mean reverent awe before God or, less often, anxiety and dread. Most interpreters take it as 'heard because of his reverence'. A minority read 'heard and delivered from his dread'. The scene is usually connected with Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, though the author does not say so.

notes.phrase: learned obedience from what he suffered
notes.note: The Greek rhymes: emathen ('he learned') and epathen ('he suffered'). The pairing was a familiar saying in Greek literature, that suffering teaches. The author applies the commonplace to the Son, who might have been expected to be exempt from it.

The verb means to bring something to its goal or completion. In Hebrews it describes Jesus being fully fitted for his priestly role through suffering and exaltation, not the removal of a moral flaw, which 4:15 rules out. In the Greek Old Testament the same word-family is used for the consecration of priests, and some scholars hear that overtone here.

The Greek pronoun can be masculine ('about him', meaning Melchizedek or Christ) or neuter ('about this', meaning the subject of Christ's priesthood). Either fits the context, and translations are divided.

notes.traditional: that one teach you; someone to teach you
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts were written without accents, and the Greek word here can be accented to mean either 'someone' or 'what'. The second reading gives 'you need to be taught what the first elements are'. The edition translated here prints the first, and the difference in meaning is slight.

The phrase can mean teaching about righteousness, the Christian message as a whole, or reasoning about what is right, which would suit the next verse's 'distinguish good from evil'. Some also see an idiom for mature, properly formed speech, in contrast to an infant's. The literal rendering is kept because the Greek does not settle the question.

notes.traditional: by reason of use; by constant practice
notes.note: English versions have long rendered this word as 'practice' or 'use', as though the mature became so by exercise. In Greek of the period, however, the word regularly means a state or condition of body or mind, the result of training and not the process. Lexical study in recent decades has favored that sense here, and recent lexicons give 'state of maturity'. The idea of training is carried by the next phrase, 'faculties trained'.

candidates.reason: A key verb across Hebrews (and in John, Paul, 1 John) where 'perfect', 'complete' and 'bring to its goal' compete and variation would obscure the letter's argument.
Rendered 'perfect', 'mature' or 'complete' by different translators across Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, and it needs coordinating with τελειόω.
The refrain 'order of Melchizedek' recurs through Hebrews 5–7 and must be uniform; 'order' versus 'kind/manner' is a real lexical choice.
Occurs in Galatians, Colossians, Hebrews and 2 Peter with disputed senses (rudiments, elemental principles, elemental spirits, physical elements), so the sense-by-sense renderings need fixing.
Recurs in Acts 7:38, Romans 3:2 and 1 Peter 4:11; 'oracles', 'words' and 'utterances' are all in use and 'oracles' may carry pagan associations for modern readers.
